article.title: More Than Ball Fields
article.author: Bill Gould
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. For generations of Altadena families, Charles S. Farnsworth Park has been much more than ballfields at the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains. It has been one of the places where Altadena comes together. Children learned to throw and catch there, parents watched from the stands, coaches became mentors and neighbors became friends. But Farnsworth has always served a broader community. Its playgrounds, tennis and pickleball courts and basketball courts provided recreation for all ages. The historic Davies Building and amphitheater hosted plays, concerts, voting and community celebrations. Farnsworth was not simply a park; it was part of Altadena’s civic life. As someone whose family lost our home and all of our belongings in the Eaton Fire, I have spent much of the past year thinking and writing about what genuine recovery should mean. I have argued that rebuilding must be centered on people and that survivors should not be left to navigate recovery alone. For many families, this process will take years. That is why rebuilding places like Farnsworth matters. Before the fire, I wrote about my family’s experience with baseball in Altadena. Our son grew up playing with Central Altadena Little League (C.A.L.L.) and the Altadena Baseball Academy, much of it at Farnsworth. I described the park as a “truly picturesque backdrop,” with the San Gabriel Mountains giving Altadena baseball a home-field advantage that had little to do with the scoreboard. Related: Rebuilding After the Eaton Fire: Disaster Recovery Isn’t Working. Here’s What Survivors Really Need The Eaton Fire devastated Altadena in January 2025, destroying thousands of homes and severely damaging Farnsworth. C.A.L.L. suddenly found itself without its longtime home. Yet baseball became one way Altadena refused to surrender its sense of community. That did not happen by accident. C.A.L.L.’s board and league leaders — many of whom lost homes or were displaced — made the remarkable decision to keep the league going. Working with coaches, parents, donors and neighboring leagues that offered fields, they put together a 2025 season and created some normalcy for children experiencing extraordinary disruption. That story became the documentary Going for Home. The Los Angeles Dodgers Foundation’s announcement that it will invest $1.4 million to restore two fields at Farnsworth therefore represents something larger than a sports construction project. Dodgers Dreamfields 69 and 70 will include improved playing surfaces and irrigation, fencing, shade structures, solar-powered scoreboards modeled after those at Dodger Stadium and a STEM Trail incorporating the foundation’s Science of Baseball curriculum. Groundbreaking is scheduled for Nov. 5. For Los Angeles Dodgers Foundation CEO Nichol McKenzie-Whiteman, the devastation gave the organization’s work a different meaning. “The Los Angeles Dodgers Foundation has been revitalizing baseball fields since 2003, but we’ve never had to restore fields due to events like the ones that occurred last year,” McKenzie-Whiteman said. “For me, it put our work in a new light; we’re restoring places that held deep sentimental value for generations of families who gathered and played in these parks.” Norma Garcia, Director of the County of Los Angeles Department of Parks and Recreation, asked the Dodgers Foundation to help with Altadena’s parks. Her department also raised $100,000 from DICK’S Sporting Goods to help pay for stands and shade — important additions for families spending hours at the fields. Garcia said the County has requested FEMA assistance for Farnsworth but, so far, has received no FEMA help for the park. Garcia described the new fields as representing “hope, healing, and renewed opportunities” for Altadena’s young people and families. For Matthew Milton, whose family has deep roots in C.A.L.L., the announcement carries special significance. “This is a blessing,” Milton said. “I’m glad the history of Jackie Robinson from this area has led the Dodgers Foundation to make this meaningful contribution to Altadena.” That connection is fitting. Jackie Robinson’s roots in the Pasadena-Altadena area are an important part of the region’s African American history. C.A.L.L. has also reflected Altadena’s rich African American and Latino history, with generations of players, families and coaches sharing the fields and sustaining youth baseball in the community. The Dreamfields connect that history to another generation of children — perhaps another Jackie Robinson among them — who need places to play, gather and simply be children. C.A.L.L. President Phillip Pollerana said Altadena is excited to get Farnsworth operating again. For Little League families — and a community filled with Dodgers fans — the Dodgers organization’s investment carries practical and symbolic meaning. Dart Cathirell, founder of the Altadena Baseball Academy, is especially pleased the project will include new scoreboards and shaded stands. Cathirell and his coaches have spent years providing young players with instruction, mentorship and opportunities to develop their skills and love of baseball. Those details — scoreboards, shade, fencing and quality playing surfaces — might seem small compared with the enormous challenge of rebuilding Altadena. They are not. Recovery is not simply the reconstruction of houses. Parks, schools, churches, libraries, ballfields and local businesses are connective tissue. They transform a collection of houses into a community. Restoring them gives displaced families another reason to return and gives children back places that defined their lives before the fire. We have already seen that power at Loma Alta Park. Its two Dodgers Dreamfields gave C.A.L.L. a place to play while Farnsworth remained unusable. The 2025 season became extraordinary: Central Altadena’s Braves won the District 17 Tournament of Champions, the first division championship in league history. Altadena’s recovery cannot be measured only by building permits or reconstructed houses. It must also be measured by whether families return, longtime institutions survive, children have safe places to play and neighbors again have places to engage one another.The Dodgers Foundation’s investment cannot solve all of Altadena’s rebuilding challenges. But it demonstrates what meaningful partnership can look like: listening to residents, investing substantial resources and building something intended to endure after the immediate disaster response has faded. Children will run onto the fields at Farnsworth again. Parents will settle into shaded stands. Baseballs will hit gloves, runs will illuminate new scoreboards, and coaches will teach another generation the game. Beyond the ballfields, families will return to Farnsworth’s playgrounds and courts and community life will return to the Davies Building and amphitheater. Against the San Gabriel Mountains, Farnsworth can once again become a place where Altadena gathers. For a community rebuilding from unimaginable loss, we should expect that future, invest in it and work together to make it happen. It will mean a piece of Altadena has returned home.
